Figure 1:Keep the route, adapt the execution.A robot leads a language-designated tourist to the departure terminal along a planned route.
The sequence shows (1) normal leading, (2) slowing down as the follower pauses for a phone call, (3) waiting while the follower briefly disengages to interact with another pedestrian, and (4) resuming afterward.
The nominal route remains unchanged, while the robot adapts how it executes the route to the follower’s evolving behavior.
Figure 2:Route–follower entanglement.Direct trajectory prediction may distort the nominal route when reacting to follower behavior.

Figure 3:Overview of LeadVLA.Temporal front/rear observations, language, and route context produce 24 shared action queries.
The route is also retained as an explicit Path reference.
Pace regulates route progress, Residual provides local adaptation, and selected follower semantics couple only to Residual.
A deterministic Path Composer outputs the final robot-local waypoints.

Figure 4:Overview of LeadInfra.LeadInfra compositionally combines route geometry, scenes, follower behaviors, appearances, and target–distractor configurations to generate diverse closed-loop robot-leading episodes.
A causal expert converts realized interaction consequences into robot-action supervision without directly observing hidden behavior programs.

Figure 5:Progressive LeadBench evaluation.Columns increase route-execution difficulty from clean conditions (Core) to moderate (Easy) and stronger interference (Constrained); rows compare single-person leading with multi-person cases containing distractors. The progression increasingly couples local route recovery with follower-aware control.

Figure 6:Real-world evaluation settings.The physical experiments retain the core interaction structure of LeadBench: Core evaluates clean route execution, Easy adds local route interference, and multi-person settings include a distractor.

header: Appendix BLeadInfra: Interaction Supervision for Robot Leading

images.caption:
Figure 7:Representative assets in LeadInfra.LeadInfra combines diverse indoor and outdoor environments with multiple robot embodiments, compositional human appearances, sensing modalities, and physical scene assets.
These assets support the route, interaction, and scene variations introduced in the following sections.

Figure 8:Dynamic referent reassignment in LeadInfra.The designated follower changes from Target A to Target B while both people remain in the scene and the nominal route is unchanged.
After reassignment, subsequent robot behavior should depend on the newly designated follower.
Colored boxes and identity labels are shown only for visualization and are never provided to the policy.

Figure 9:LeadInfra scene composition and episode generation.Starting from diverse environments (Sec.B.1), LeadInfra samples a nominal route (Sec.B.2),
instantiates robot and human actors, composes follower-interaction programs and local scene variation
(Secs.B.3andB.4), and executes the resulting task in closed loop.
A causal expert (Sec.B.5) generates robot supervision from realized interaction evidence rather than directly from hidden follower programs.

header: Appendix DExperimental Details and Additional Results

images.caption:
Figure 10:Human-expert teleoperation interface.Operators control the robot online while observing the same front/rear visual inputs, language instruction, and nominal route information available to evaluated policies.
No simulator-privileged state is exposed through the interface.

header: Appendix EReal-World Evaluation and Qualitative Analysis

images.caption:
Figure 11:Real-robot platform.LeadVLA is deployed on a Unitree G1 equipped with front- and rear-facing
Intel RealSense D455 cameras.
Only RGB observations are provided to the policy; depth is retained for
offline evaluation.

Figure 12:Representative real-world closed-loop sequences.Rows correspond to Core-S, Core-M, Easy-S, and Easy-M.
The overlaid speed gauge visualizes changes in the robot’s execution response over time.
Across settings, LeadVLA largely preserves route-level progress while adapting its execution to the designated follower and local route conditions.

Figure 13:Referent-conditioned control in the real world.The physical setting and nominal route remain unchanged while the language instruction designates Target A (top) or Target B (bottom).
LeadVLA changes its execution according to the currently designated follower, showing transfer of referent-aware control without real-world policy fine-tuning.
Colored target annotations are added only for visualization and are never provided to the policy.

Figure 14:Ignoring distractor behavior during real-world leading.Target A remains the designated follower throughout the sequence.
The distractor begins to lag, stops, and eventually falls substantially
behind in the later frames, while LeadVLA continues leading Target A
without slowing or waiting for the distractor.
The speed gauge visualizes the robot’s execution response over time.
